tldr: Evaluating five commercial mobile robots under a common protocol using a laser tracker (ground truth accuracy of approximately 6 µm) revealed that no platform can meet aerospace non-destructive evaluation (NDE) tolerances (±0.2 to 1.0 mm) on its base alone, and that positioning accuracy directly mirrors the hierarchy of localisation capabilities.
hero_caption: The five commercial mobile platforms evaluated in this study (top left to right: MiR250, Boston Dynamics Spot, KUKA KMR; bottom left to right: KUKA KMP-1500, Clearpath Husky). Robots with diverse locomotion mechanisms and localisation methods—differential drive, omnidirectional Mecanum wheels, and quadrupedal walking—were compared under identical conditions.
overview:
Non-destructive evaluation (NDE) of large-scale structures such as aircraft and pressure vessels has traditionally relied on fixed industrial robots offering sub-millimetre precision (around 0.1 mm). However, fixed cells lack flexibility and reach their limits when scanning massive structures. Mobile manipulators, which mount a manipulator arm onto an autonomous mobile robot (AMR), are a promising alternative. Yet, the primary bottleneck is uncertainty over how accurate and repeatable the mobile base itself truly is. Existing standards (such as ISO) focus primarily on obstacle detection and collision avoidance, leaving no standardised protocol for evaluating millimetre-level positioning accuracy.

To address this gap, the authors developed a shared evaluation workflow using an external reference system: the Leica Absolute Tracker AT901, with an accuracy of approximately 6 µm. By placing optical retroreflectors on the four corners of each platform, they formulated a coupled calibration method to solve for the transformation between the laser coordinate frame and the robot coordinate frame. Five representative commercial platforms (KUKA KMP-1500, KUKA KMR, MiR250, Boston Dynamics Spot, and Clearpath Husky) were run along an identical path in the same experimental environment, thoroughly measuring both static positioning accuracy and dynamic trajectory-following accuracy.

Static positioning error ranged from a median of 8.2 mm for the newest LiDAR SLAM platform (KMP-1500) to 63.5 mm for Spot using only onboard visual odometry. The wheel-odometry-only Husky drifted so severely that it could not be calibrated. No mobile platform met the ±0.2 to 1.0 mm tolerance required in aerospace NDE on its base alone, concretely quantifying the scale of error that supplementary end-effector sensing or external metrology must overcome.
contributions: Established a high-precision experimental workflow using a laser tracker (~6 µm accuracy) as an external ground truth to evaluate base-positioning accuracy across heterogeneous commercial mobile robots under a common protocol.

Provided a quantitative benchmark of static and dynamic trajectory-following accuracy for five representative commercial robots, capturing distribution tails rather than relying solely on single-value means.

Demonstrated a 'Localisation Cascade', where differences in localisation algorithms and sensor suites—from modern LiDAR SLAM down to pure dead reckoning—directly dictate positioning accuracy and external calibration success.

Showed that mobile bases alone fall short of aerospace NDE requirements (±0.2 to 1.0 mm) by roughly one to two orders of magnitude, providing quantitative design inputs to size the supplementary sensing required to bridge this gap.

sections.heading: Why do we need a definitive test of mobile base accuracy now?
sections.summary: Precise positioning is essential for non-destructive evaluation in aerospace, such as placing ultrasonic probes, but traditional fixed robots cannot easily inspect large structures. While flexible mobile manipulators are increasingly attractive, standardised data and protocols for evaluating base-positioning uncertainty have been critically lacking.
sections.details:
Non-destructive evaluation (NDE) is critical for quality assurance in high-integrity structures such as aircraft, pressure vessels, and wind turbine blades. Aerospace components adhere to exceptionally strict safety standards, requiring inspection data (such as ultrasonic testing measurements) to be registered to 3D CAD models with millimetre-level spatial accuracy. Conventional fixed industrial robots easily satisfy this requirement with repeatability around 0.1 mm. However, they are confined to fixed work cells, making them unsuitable for inspecting structures spanning several to tens of metres.

Consequently, mobile manipulators that place a robotic arm on a mobile base have gained substantial attention. Moving freely, they offer flexible inspection across large structures without requiring exhaustive prior geometric setup. However, end-effector positioning accuracy is fundamentally bounded by the base. If base positioning deviates by several centimetres, the arm cannot reach its intended inspection point, regardless of its own internal precision.

Current ISO standards for robotic NDE and service robots focus primarily on collision avoidance and operational safety. They do not cover evaluation methods for positioning accuracy and repeatability required in precision tasks. This study directly compares static and dynamic positioning accuracy across five commercial platforms representing distinct locomotion and sensing designs (KUKA KMP-1500, KUKA KMR, MiR250, Boston Dynamics Spot, Clearpath Husky) under an identical external reference protocol.

captions.P2: The KUKA KMR mobile manipulator platform. It integrates a high-precision KUKA LBR iiwa collaborative arm atop an omnidirectional Mecanum-wheeled base, but exploiting that end-effector precision requires accurate base localisation.

sections.heading: Navigation advances and the overlooked challenge of physical accuracy testing
sections.summary: While SLAM and sensor fusion have greatly expanded AMR capabilities, most validation has remained confined to simulation. High-precision real-world ground-truth measurement techniques and standardised comparative frameworks have historically been missing.
sections.details:
### Advances in Navigation and Path Planning
Mobile robot navigation combines dead reckoning odometry (wheel encoders or leg kinematics) with SLAM (Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping) using external perception sensors such as LiDAR and cameras. Because raw odometry drifts over time due to wheel slip, modern industrial AMRs typically fuse LiDAR scan matching, visual odometry, and IMU data. Global and local path planning algorithms have matured significantly, making safe obstacle avoidance a solved industrial capability.

### The Research Gap in Precision Evaluation
However, navigation research has focused largely on collision-free goal arrival and map consistency, rarely probing millimetre-level positioning accuracy. Furthermore, much of this work relies on simulation, abstracting away real-world physics such as wheel-floor friction variance, structural inertia under heavy payloads, and mechanical backlash.

Acquiring sub-millimetre ground truth in the physical world demands expensive metrology, such as motion capture systems or laser trackers. Prior evaluations using planar fiducials (AR tags) suffered from sensor noise floors around 1.4 mm, limiting evaluation fidelity. In addition, manufacturer specification sheets use disparate testing methods, preventing apples-to-apples comparison. What has been sorely needed is a way to isolate and measure true platform positioning accuracy—incorporating mechanics, sensors, and control stacks—against an external reference.

sections.heading: A unified calibration protocol using a 6 µm laser tracker across diverse platforms
sections.summary: Using a Leica laser tracker with ~6 µm accuracy, the authors designed a framework to calibrate and benchmark five platforms with completely different internal coordinate frames. They formulated a multi-corner calibration model, rigorous outlier rejection, and decomposed dynamic path tracking.
sections.details:
### Target Platforms and Test Environment
The study selected five distinct platforms: the differential-drive MiR250, KUKA KMP-1500, and Clearpath Husky; the quadrupedal Boston Dynamics Spot; and the omnidirectional Mecanum-drive KUKA KMR. The Husky used only wheel odometry, Spot relied exclusively on onboard visual odometry (stock configuration without an add-on LiDAR), and the remaining three used LiDAR SLAM. Tests were conducted in a 5 m × 10 m arena, where each platform navigated a rectangular trajectory (5 m along the X-axis, 2 m along the Y-axis). Robots were configured to perform point turns at corners to minimise turning-mode discrepancies.

### Coordinate Calibration Formulation
Ground truth was recorded with a Leica Absolute Tracker AT901 3DOF interferometric tracker (~6 µm positioning accuracy). Because the robot's self-reported pose (map frame) and the tracker readings (laser frame) use completely independent origins, and the physical offsets from the robot centre to the mounted SMRs (Spherically Mounted Retroreflectors) are unmeasured, the laser-frame reflector position $^L P_{reflector}$ was modelled as:

$$^L P_{reflector} = {^L R_R} \cdot ({^R R_{robot}} \cdot {^B d_{reflector}} + {^R P_{center}}) + {^L T_R}$$

Here, $^L R_R$ and $^L T_R$ represent the rotation matrix and translation vector from the map to the laser frame, $^R R_{robot}$ and $^R P_{center}$ denote the robot's reported pose, and $^B d_{reflector}$ represents the rigid offset vector of each reflector. By placing reflectors at all four corners, the resulting overdetermined system with 18 unknown parameters was solved simultaneously via ordinary least squares using L-BFGS-B optimization.

### Measurement Validation and Dynamic Tracking
The static measurement noise floor of the laser tracker was just 7.0 µm (3D standard deviation), far below the robots' millimetre-scale errors. Robust estimation via RANSAC confirmed the dataset was free of gross transmission anomalies, flagging only a single spurious data point across all platforms (on the MiR250).
For dynamic evaluation over 10 laps of the rectangular path, robots and the tracker ran on independent clocks and varying telemetry rates, ruling out tight temporal alignment. Therefore, tracking errors were decomposed along trajectory segments into 'cross-track error' (orthogonal to heading) and 'along-track error' (parallel to heading). Cross-track error is insensitive to timestamp latency, serving as an uncorrupted metric of dynamic path-following accuracy.

sections.heading: Beyond the spec sheets: From 8.2 mm median error to uncalibratable drift
sections.summary: Static positioning median error varied from 8.2 mm on the KMP-1500 to 63.5 mm on Spot, while the odometry-only Husky drifted so severely it could not be calibrated. Dynamic cross-track errors followed the exact same hierarchy, showing that underlying localisation methods dictate accuracy.
sections.details:
### Static Positioning Accuracy
Static 3D Euclidean errors clearly separated the platforms by their localisation capabilities:
- **KUKA KMP-1500**: Achieved the highest accuracy, with a median error of 8.2 mm (mean 8.7 mm, 95% CI 7.7–9.8 mm) and a planar spread $\sigma_{2D}$ of 8.9 mm. However, 41.7% of poses exceeded 10 mm error, displaying a heavy right-tail distribution.
- **MiR250**: Median error was 24.9 mm (mean 25.6 mm). With 249 static samples, its confidence interval was narrow, demonstrating a consistent systematic bias of roughly 2.5 cm.
- **KUKA KMR**: Median error was 34.1 mm (mean 39.0 mm). Despite sharing KUKA LiDAR SLAM lineage, it performed 4 to 5 times worse than the KMP-1500, with 100% of points exceeding 10 mm error.
- **Boston Dynamics Spot**: Median error was 63.5 mm (mean 77.3 mm). Operating purely on visual odometry, it showed substantial anisotropic error (35 mm along X vs 82 mm along Y).
- **Clearpath Husky**: With uncorrected wheel odometry, positional drift grew unbounded, preventing convergence of the rigid-body transformation and rendering it 'Uncalibrated'.

### Dynamic Path-Following Accuracy
Dynamic cross-track errors mirrored the static rankings. The KMP-1500 achieved tight path tracking with a mean cross-track error of 6.9 mm (median 6.2 mm), and its 50 Hz logging rate kept along-track error down to 7.5 mm. In contrast, the KMR (mean 17.6 mm) and MiR250 (mean 18.5 mm) performed similarly to each other. Spot exhibited pronounced snaking, averaging 112.1 mm (median 105.9 mm) with wide variability between segments (110 ± 66 mm).
On platforms with lower logging rates (such as KMR and MiR250), temporal latency produced apparent square-wave artifacts of 200 to 300 mm in the along-track direction, demonstrating the necessity of separating cross-track from along-track components.

sections.heading: Mobile bases cannot meet aerospace NDE alone: How to size the sensing gap
sections.summary: Compared to fixed industrial robots (0.01 to 0.2 mm) and aerospace tolerances (±0.2 to 1.0 mm), autonomous mobile bases fall short by one to two orders of magnitude. This does not preclude mobile bases from NDE, but establishes exact performance requirements for supplementary end-effector sensing.
sections.details:
### The Localisation Cascade
These findings show that platform accuracy is governed primarily by sensor modalities and localisation software generation rather than platform footprint or brand. The 4-to-5-fold performance gap between the KUKA KMP-1500 and KUKA KMR—two robots from the same manufacturer using LiDAR SLAM—highlights how drive kinematics and controller implementations create substantial divergence.

### Implications for Aerospace NDE
Aerospace NDE standards require inspection tolerances of ±0.2 to 1.0 mm. The best-performing platform (KMP-1500, 8.7 mm mean static error) misses this requirement by roughly an order of magnitude, while Spot (77.3 mm) misses by nearly two orders. Compared to fixed manipulators (0.01 to 0.2 mm), gaining mobility degrades raw base accuracy by two to four orders of magnitude.
However, in step-and-measure static NDE, knowing the distribution bounds allows engineers to design appropriate compensation systems. Choosing a KMP-1500 means the end-effector vision or compliance mechanism must absorb roughly one order of magnitude of error (~1 cm). Selecting a platform like Spot requires secondary sensing or long-stroke compliant fixtures capable of accommodating nearly two orders of magnitude (~10 cm).

### Cost vs. Flexibility Trade-offs
A fixed robotic cell involves substantial capital expenditure (£200k–£500k) and dedicated floor space. AMRs cost less upfront (£50k–£150k), but closing the millimetre gap with external laser trackers (£80k–£150k) or vision systems (£20k–£50k) drives the total system cost back toward a fixed installation. The business case hinges on whether operational flexibility offsets the cost of supplementary metrology.

sections.heading: A reproducible engineering baseline for deploying mobile robots in precision tasks
sections.summary: This study evaluated base-positioning accuracy across commercial mobile platforms using a common laser-tracker protocol, uncovering a clear performance hierarchy tied to localisation capability. Rather than making raw feasibility claims, it provides reproducible design baselines to size required secondary sensing.
sections.details:
The goal of this work was not to claim that mobile platforms can independently satisfy rigorous aerospace tolerances, but to establish an objective, reproducible baseline of mobile base positioning using an external ground truth. The results quantify a wide spectrum of static capability, spanning from 8.2 mm (KMP-1500) to 63.5 mm (Spot), down to the uncalibratable drift of uncorrected odometry (Husky).

Importantly, the nature of the error differed fundamentally across platforms: the KMP-1500 demonstrated high nominal precision punctuated by a heavy tail (exceeding 10 mm in over 40% of poses), whereas the MiR250 showed a consistent, systematic offset of ~2.5 cm. This distinction dictates deployment strategy: the former requires in-situ end-effector verification at each pose, while the latter can be mitigated via a constant software offset calibration.

Future work will look toward hardware-triggered microsecond clock synchronisation (such as PTP), deploying identical open-source SLAM pipelines across heterogeneous chassis to isolate purely mechanical kinematics, and evaluating dynamic payload shifts when carrying integrated manipulator arms.

takeaways: Commercial mobile base positioning accuracy ranges from millimetres to centimetres (8.2 mm on the KMP-1500, 63.5 mm on Spot); sub-millimetre precision tasks require supplementary end-effector sensing.

Even within the same brand and LiDAR SLAM classification, hardware generations and drive kinematics can cause a 4-to-5-fold difference in accuracy (KMP-1500 vs KMR), making empirical benchmarking essential over spec sheets.
Evaluating dynamic trajectory error requires decoupling cross-track error (orthogonal path adherence) from along-track error, which is heavily distorted by time synchronisation latency.

Error profiles vary fundamentally across platforms (systematic static bias vs long-tailed distributions), requiring different mitigation strategies (fixed offset calibration vs continuous in-situ measurement feedback).
limitations: Due to the acceptance angle limitations of the laser tracker's SMR spherically mounted retroreflectors, robots had to stop at corners for manual reflector reorientation, preventing continuous dynamic assessment of high-speed turning kinematics.

The absence of hardware clock synchronisation between robot controllers and the laser tracker required velocity-profile interpolation, leaving residual uncertainty in along-track dynamic errors during acceleration and deceleration.

Platforms were evaluated with their proprietary software stacks (native SLAM and visual odometry), meaning kinematic chassis performance could not be decoupled entirely from software and algorithmic differences.
